fields.claim_quote: A graph contains a cycle if and only if there is a cut with more than one edge.
fields.explanation: The claim asserts "G contains a cycle IFF G has a cut with more than one edge", and the proof uses the direction (cut with >1 edge) => (G contains a cycle), i.e. contrapositively: in a forest every cut has at most one edge. With the standard definition of a cut (the edge set delta(S) induced by a nonempty proper vertex subset S), this is false: on P_3 = ({0,1,2}, {01,02}), the claim says |delta({0})| = 2 > 1 implies a cycle exists, but the recomputed cycle test gives |E| = 2 = |V| - c(G) = 3 - 1, so the graph is acyclic. More strongly, the exhaustive census shows the implication is near-vacuously false: EVERY graph with at least 2 edges has a bipartition cut with 2 edges (choose S containing exactly one endpoint of each of two chosen edges), so 3230 of the 3271 labelled forests on 1..6 vertices are counterexamples (the 41 non-counterexamples are exactly the forests with at most one edge). Consequently the proof step at line 0018 -- "at least one pair of edges in F_1 shares a cut; this contradicts that F_1 is a forest" -- is invalid as stated, since any two edges of any forest share some cut. The script also tested the charitable repair in which "cut" means BOND (minimal edge cut): under that reading the biconditional holds with zero failures in either direction over all 1099 labelled simple graphs on 1..5 vertices (every nonempty edge subset checked for minimal-disconnecting-set status). So the flaw is precisely the omitted minimality/bond requirement in footnote 3, not a defect that is unfixable; but the sentence as written is refuted by a 3-vertex graph.
fields.flaw: Footnote 3's biconditional "A graph contains a cycle if and only if there is a cut with more than one edge" — specifically the direction (cut with more than one edge implies a cycle), which is the direction invoked in the exchange-property proof at line 0018 ("at least one pair of edges in F_1 shares a cut; this contradicts that F_1 is a forest").
fields.problem:
Greedy choice and matroids (greedoids)

As I was going through the material about the greedy approach, I came to know that a knowledge on matroids (greedoids) will help me approaching the problem properly. After reading about matroids I have roughly understood what matroids are. But how do you use the concept of a matroid for solving a given optimisation problem? 

Take, for example, the [activity selection problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Activity_selection_problem). What are the steps to use matroid theory for solving the problem?
fields.source_context:
0014 | 
0015 |  1. To show: $(E,I)$ is a matroid. We have to verify [three properties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matroid#Independent_sets.2C_bases.2C_and_circuits):
0016 |    * $\emptyset \in I$ -- the empty graph is a forest.
0017 |    * If $F \in I$, every subset of $F$ is in $I$ -- given an arbitrary forest, *removing* edges can not introduce cycles. Therefore, every subgraph of a forest is a forest.
0018 |    * For every $F_1,F_2 \in I$, $|F_1| > |F_2|$ implies that there is $e \in F_1 \setminus F_2$ so that $F_2 \cup \{e\} \in I$ -- consider an arbitrary forest $F_1$ and a smaller one $F_2$. Assume there is no such $e$. That means that all edges in $F_1$ lie in cuts induced by edges in $F_2$³. As there are only $|F_2|$ such cuts, at least one pair of edges in $F_1$ [shares a cut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pigeon_hole_principle); this contradicts that $F_1$ is a forest.
0019 | 
0020 |  2. To show: any element $F^*$ with maximum weight in $I$ is a minimum spanning tree of $G$. First of all, it is clear $F^*$ has maximum weight according to $c'$, so by definition of $c'$, it also has *minimum* weight according to $c$. Now all we have to show is that it is a spanning tree: if it was not, it would not be maximal in the sense that we could still add edges (with positive weight), contradicting maximum weight.
0021 | 
0022 | ---
0023 | 
0024 |  1. We can deal with negative edge weights by adding the minimum weight plus one to all weights.
0025 |  2. A [forest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forest_%28graph_theory%29) is a disjoint union of trees.
0026 |  3. A graph contains a cycle if and only if there is a cut with more than one edge.
fields.witness: The path P_3 on three vertices: V = {0, 1, 2}, E = {01, 02} (equivalently any path a-b-c). It has |V| = 3, |E| = 2, and 1 connected component, so |E| = |V| - c(G) = 3 - 1 = 2, i.e. it is a forest and contains NO cycle. Take S = {0}: the cut delta(S) = {uv in E : |{u,v} cap S| = 1} = {01, 02}, so |delta(S)| = 2 > 1. Equally small alternative witnesses: E = {01, 12} with S = {1}; and the disjoint-edge forest 2K_2 on V = {0,1,2,3}, E = {01, 23}, with S = {0, 2}, giving delta(S) = {01, 23}, |delta(S)| = 2. The script prints these explicitly along with the recomputed component count, the cycle test, and the cut it found.
